screens.narratorSegment: At its heart, a progressive deployment is an evolution of traditional rolling and canary strategies. Its primary goal is to introduce new application versions to your users gradually, rather than all at once. content.html:
Module 10›Chapter 10.4›Progressive Deployments
Core Concept

The Power of Progressive Deployments

Minimizing risk through gradual, controlled rollouts.

What are Progressive Deployments?

An advanced deployment strategy that introduces new application versions incrementally to users, continuously monitoring health and performance.

  • •Evolved from rolling and canary strategies.
  • •Focuses on gradual introduction, not all-at-once.
  • •Continuously monitors health and performance.
Key Takeaway

Progressive deployments are crucial for minimizing risk, limiting the blast radius of issues, and enabling rapid, automated rollbacks in modern CI/CD.

Why They Matter

  • •Minimize Risk: Limit impact of potential bugs to a small user segment.
  • •Rapid Rollback: Automated mechanisms to revert to a stable state quickly.
  • •Enhanced Stability: Maintain service availability and performance.
  • •Continuous Feedback: Monitor real-world performance before full rollout.

Analogy: The Pilot Program

Think of a progressive deployment like a pilot program for a new product. Instead of launching to everyone at once, you release it to a small, controlled group. You gather feedback, monitor for issues, and refine the product before a wider release. This controlled approach ensures that any problems are caught early and addressed before they affect a larger audience, making the overall launch much safer and more successful.

screens.title: CodeDeploy's Blue/Green for ECS
screens.narratorSegment: When working with containerized applications on Amazon ECS, AWS CodeDeploy's blue/green deployment type serves as the inherent foundation for progressive rollouts. As you might recall, blue/green deployments involve maintaining two identical environments: the 'blue' environment running the current stable version, and the 'green' environment where the new application version is deployed. The progressive aspect comes into play with how CodeDeploy manages the traffic shift between these two environments. Instead of an immediate, all-at-once switch, CodeDeploy allows you to configure a gradual transition. This means your new 'green' task set can be thoroughly validated and monitored while the 'blue' environment continues to serve the majority of your users. This isolation significantly reduces the risk associated with new deployments, providing a safe sandbox for testing before full production exposure. It's a powerful mechanism for ensuring that your containerized applications can be updated with minimal disruption and maximum confidence. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 10›Chapter 10.4›CodeDeploy & ECS
AWS ECS Integration

CodeDeploy's Blue/Green for ECS

The foundation for progressive container deployments.

Blue/Green Deployment Overview

CodeDeploy's blue/green deployment type is inherently progressive for Amazon ECS. It involves two distinct environments:

  • •Blue Environment: Runs the current, stable application version.
  • •Green Environment: Deploys the new application version to a separate task set.

Traffic is then shifted gradually from blue to green, allowing for controlled rollouts.

Key Takeaway

CodeDeploy's blue/green deployments for ECS provide isolated environments and controlled traffic shifting, forming the basis for progressive rollouts.

screens.title: Linear Deployments with CodeDeploy
screens.narratorSegment: One of the powerful progressive deployment configurations offered by AWS CodeDeploy for ECS is the linear deployment. This strategy allows you to shift traffic to your new application version in equal increments over a specified period. For instance, you might configure CodeDeploy to shift 10% of your user traffic to the new 'green' environment every five minutes until 100% of the traffic is on the new version. This provides a highly controlled, time-based rollout, giving you predictable intervals to monitor the new version's performance and stability. The key benefit here is the ability to observe the new version's behavior under increasing load in a measured way. If any issues arise during one of these incremental shifts, you have a clear window to detect them and initiate a rollback before the problem affects a larger portion of your user base. It's a methodical approach that balances the need for rapid deployment with the imperative for stability. Linear Deployments with CodeDeploy means linear deployments shift traffic in equal increments over time, offering controlled monitoring windows.. In practical terms, shifting traffic in equal, timed increments for controlled rollouts.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Canary Deployments with CodeDeploy
screens.narratorSegment: Complementing linear deployments, CodeDeploy also offers a canary deployment configuration for ECS, which is another powerful progressive strategy. With a canary deployment, traffic is shifted in two distinct increments. First, a small percentage of traffic, perhaps 10%, is routed to the new 'green' environment. This initial, small group of users acts as a 'canary in the coal mine,' providing early feedback on the new version's stability and performance without impacting the majority of your users. After a specified wait time, during which you can rigorously monitor and test, the remaining traffic, typically 90%, is then shifted to the new version. This two-phase approach is ideal for high-risk changes or when you want to validate a new feature with a real-world subset of users before committing to a full rollout. It's a strategic way to minimize risk by catching potential issues early, ensuring a smoother and more confident transition to your new application version. screens.title: CloudWatch Alarms for Automated Rollback
screens.narratorSegment: A critical component of any progressive deployment strategy, especially with AWS CodeDeploy, is the integration of Amazon CloudWatch alarms for automated rollbacks. During the traffic shifting phases of a linear or canary deployment, CodeDeploy can continuously monitor critical metrics from your new 'green' environment. These metrics might include HTTP 5xx errors, application latency, or C P U utilization. You configure CloudWatch alarms to trigger if any of these metrics breach predefined thresholds. If an alarm goes into an 'ALARM' state during a traffic shift, CodeDeploy can automatically initiate a rollback, reverting all traffic to the original, stable 'blue' environment. This automated safety mechanism is paramount for maintaining service stability and preventing widespread impact from faulty deployments. While the appspec. yaml defines deployment hooks, the actual progressive traffic shifting and rollback alarms are primarily configured within the CodeDeploy Deployment Group settings, where you explicitly link your CloudWatch alarms. This ensures that your deployments are not just progressive, but also self-healing and resilient. CloudWatch Alarms for Automated Rollback means cloudwatch alarms monitor new deployments and automatically trigger rollbacks if critical metrics breach thresholds.. In practical terms, ensuring stability with proactive monitoring during progressive deployments.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 10›Chapter 10.4›Automated Rollbacks
Safety Mechanism

CloudWatch Alarms for Automated Rollback

Ensuring stability with proactive monitoring during progressive deployments.

How Automated Rollbacks Work

  • •CodeDeploy monitors the new 'green' environment during traffic shifts.
  • •CloudWatch alarms are configured to watch critical metrics (e.g., 5xx errors, latency).
  • •If an alarm triggers, CodeDeploy automatically reverts traffic to the 'blue' environment.

This mechanism is configured in the CodeDeploy Deployment Group, linking specific CloudWatch alarms.

Key Takeaway

CloudWatch alarms provide an essential automated safety net, triggering immediate rollbacks to prevent widespread impact from deployment issues.

screens.title: Progressive Deployments in Amazon EKS
screens.narratorSegment: While CodeDeploy excels with ECS, progressive deployments in Amazon EKS, or Elastic Kubernetes Service, often leverage Kubernetes native constructs or specialized tools. By default, Kubernetes Deployments support what are known as 'rolling updates.' This means that when you update your application, Kubernetes gradually replaces old Pods with new ones, ensuring continuous availability. You can fine-tune this process using parameters like max Unavailable and max Surge to control the rollout speed and capacity. For example, max Unavailable dictates how many Pods can be unavailable during an update, while max Surge specifies how many new Pods can be created above the desired replica count. While CodeDeploy can deploy to EKS, it's typically used for broader application deployments rather than the fine-grained traffic management within the cluster itself. Understanding these native capabilities is your first step towards mastering progressive rollouts in a Kubernetes environment, setting the stage for more advanced strategies. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 10›Chapter 10.4›EKS Deployments
EKS Strategies

Progressive Deployments in Amazon EKS

Leveraging Kubernetes native capabilities and AWS tools.

Kubernetes Rolling Updates (Default)

  • •Gradually replaces old Pods with new ones.
  • •Ensures continuous application availability.
  • •Controlled by maxUnavailable (how many can be down) and maxSurge (how many extra can be up).

CodeDeploy can deploy to EKS, but fine-grained traffic management is often handled by Kubernetes-native tools.

Key Takeaway

Kubernetes' rolling updates provide a default progressive deployment, while CodeDeploy focuses on broader application orchestration for EKS.

Kubernetes Deployment Snippet
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: my-app
spec:
  replicas: 3
  strategy:

At its heart, a progressive deployment is an evolution of traditional rolling and canary strategies. Its primary goal is to introduce new application versions to your users gradually, rather than all at once. Imagine you're launching a new feature; instead of exposing it to your entire user base immediately, you roll it out to a small percentage first. This approach allows you to continuously monitor the health and performance of the new version in a real-world environment, limiting the 'blast radius' of any potential issues. As you might recall, blue/green deployments involve maintaining two identical environments: the 'blue' environment running the current stable version, and the 'green' environment where the new application version is deployed. The progressive aspect comes into play with how CodeDeploy manages the traffic shift between these two environments. Instead of an immediate, all-at-once switch, CodeDeploy allows you to configure a gradual transition. This means your new 'green' task set can be thoroughly validated and monitored while the 'blue' environment continues to serve the majority of your users. This isolation significantly reduces the risk associated with new deployments, providing a safe sandbox for testing before full production exposure.
